texto:
Satellite TV is television delivered from a satellite in orbit to a receiving dish at the viewer's home or business, with no cable or terrestrial transmitter in between. It exists because one satellite can cover a continent: a broadcaster or pay-TV operator sends channels up once and every household inside the satellite's footprint can receive them, including farms far from any cable line. The consumer service is called direct-to-home (DTH) or, in the United States, direct broadcast satellite (DBS).
How the signal gets from uplink to living room
The chain starts at an uplink centre, where the operator gathers channels, compresses them, encrypts the paid tiers and transmits them to a satellite. Nearly all television satellites sit in geostationary orbit, about 35,785 kilometres (22,236 miles) above the equator, according to Encyclopaedia Britannica. At that height a satellite circles once every 23 hours and 56 minutes, matching the rotation of the Earth, so it appears fixed in the sky and a dish can stay bolted in one position.
Each satellite carries transponders, which receive the uplinked signal, shift it to a different frequency and beam it back down. Consumer DBS in the United States uses the Ku band between 12.2 and 12.7 GHz at power levels that can exceed 100 watts, according to the Museum of Broadcast Communications' encyclopedia, which is why an 18-inch dish suffices; the older C-band service needed dishes six to eight feet across. At the home, a low-noise block downconverter (LNB) at the dish's focal point amplifies the faint signal and converts it to a lower frequency that can travel down coaxial cable to a set-top box. The box unscrambles paid channels only if its smart card or key passes the operator's conditional access check.
Transmission standards set how much fits on each transponder. Europe and much of the world use the DVB-S family from the Digital Video Broadcasting Project. DVB-S2, ratified by ETSI as EN 302 307 in March 2005, carries about 30 per cent more data than the original DVB-S on the same bandwidth and power, and an extension known as DVB-S2X followed in March 2014.
Satellite has two structural weaknesses. The signal travels roughly 72,000 kilometres up and back, so it arrives a fraction of a second behind terrestrial feeds, and heavy rain or snow can attenuate Ku-band signals enough to freeze the picture, a problem engineers call rain fade. It is also one-way: interactive features, viewing data and on-demand libraries depend on a separate internet connection to the box.
Where advertising enters a one-way pipe
Most commercials on satellite are national spots passed through unchanged. Like cable operators, satellite distributors receive a small allocation of time each hour to sell themselves, the local avails described in PPC Land's MVPD explainer. In the United States the sellers are DirecTV Advertising and Dish Media.
Targeting different households with different ads is harder on satellite than on cable, because every home receives the identical downlink. The workaround is to send the ads ahead of time. DirecTV and Dish store addressable spots on the hard drive of the digital video recorder inside the set-top box, typically about 4 GB or 600 to 800 ads, refreshed on a 72-hour cycle, according to Tom Morgan, founder of BlackArrow, speaking to Digiday in 2019. When a break begins, the box plays the stored ad assigned to that household in place of the broadcast one. Only about two of the roughly 16 hourly ad minutes were addressable then, Morgan said. Cablevision, DirecTV and Dish launched household addressable advertising commercially in 2012. Sky in Britain used the same model when it launched AdSmart in January 2014, initially across about a fifth of UK homes, according to The Drum.
Return-path data from satellite receivers also feeds measurement. Nielsen's Big Data + Panel currency, which took effect in September 2025, combines a 42,000-home panel with inputs from 45 million households, including cable set-top boxes and satellite receivers.
From Clarke's relays to two American giants
The idea predates the hardware. Arthur C. Clarke described geostationary relay satellites for radio and television in "Extra-Terrestrial Relays", published in Wireless World in 1945. Telstar 1, built by Bell Telephone Laboratories for AT&T, launched on July 10, 1962 and carried the first live television pictures across the Atlantic that month.
Satellite became a television business through cable. On September 30, 1975, HBO used satellite to deliver the Muhammad Ali-Joe Frazier fight known as the "Thrilla in Manila" to cable systems. "Going up on the satellite was really the impetus for all the programming we see today," Jerry Levin, then HBO's president, later told Multichannel News. Rural households bought large C-band dishes to pick up the same feeds, and programmers began scrambling them in 1985.
Congress gave satellite operators a legal basis to carry broadcast networks through the Satellite Home Viewer Act of 1988, which created a six-year compulsory copyright licence for distant network signals. The modern small-dish industry followed. Hughes launched the first DirecTV satellite on December 17, 1993, and the first customer signed up on June 17, 1994, paying $699 for the dish and receiver, according to Sound & Vision. EchoStar's first satellite launched on December 28, 1995, and Dish Network served its first broadcast customers in March 1996, according to EchoStar. In Europe, SES launched Astra 1A on December 11, 1988 and Sky Television started its four-channel package on it on February 5, 1989.
Regulation shaped the product. The Satellite Home Viewer Improvement Act of November 1999 allowed "local-into-local" service, in which satellite operators retransmit local broadcast stations back into their own markets using spot beams. The Television Viewer Protection Act, signed on December 20, 2019, made the distant-signal licence permanent but largely conditioned it on local service in all 210 Nielsen markets, which Dish provided and DirecTV did not, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Why it matters to marketers
In many rural areas satellite remains the only multichannel option, which gives it reach that cable and streaming cannot fully replicate. DirecTV and Dish together held nearly 16 per cent of US multichannel subscriptions around 2001, against about 80 per cent for cable, according to the Museum of Broadcast Communications. The footprint still matters for addressable buying: satellite is one of four delivery environments for addressable campaigns listed in the Video Advertising Bureau's 2026 addressable TV guide.
In parts of Europe the medium is larger still. In Poland, satellite accounted for 29.6 per cent of total TV viewing time in July 2024, behind cable at 32.6 per cent. SES reported in 2023 that its satellites reached 369 million TV homes worldwide, 175.8 million of them in Europe.
Decline, debt and contested features
The subscriber base is shrinking. US satellite TV lost a combined 399,000 subscribers in the first quarter of 2026, according to Light Reading. EchoStar ended the second quarter of 2026 with 4.68 million Dish TV satellite customers, down from 4.84 million three months earlier. India's pay DTH base fell to 48.56 million on June 30, 2026, according to the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India, a figure that excludes the free platform DD Free Dish.
Consolidation has repeatedly failed. The Department of Justice sued on October 31, 2002 to block EchoStar's acquisition of DirecTV's parent, Hughes Electronics. "This merger would give Echostar control of the skies for the provision of video programming by satellite," said Charles A. James, then assistant attorney general. A second attempt, in which DirecTV agreed on September 30, 2024 to take Dish and Sling TV for $1 plus about $9.75 billion of debt, was terminated on November 22, 2024 after Dish bondholders rejected a debt exchange. Craig Moffett of MoffettNathanson has argued that savings would be limited because the two use different conditional access systems, according to Light Reading.
Operators have also clashed with the networks whose ads they carry. Dish's AutoHop feature, which skipped commercials in recorded primetime shows, drew lawsuits from CBS, NBC and Fox in May 2012. Dish settled with Fox in February 2016, agreeing to disable skipping on Fox shows for seven days after first airing, according to informitv.
Not the same as
- Cable TV delivers the same channels over coaxial or fibre lines from a headend. Cable is two-way and can switch ads in real time.
- Satellite internet, such as Hughes or Starlink, carries broadband data, not packaged channels. Starlink's low earth orbit satellites have latency of 20 to 40 milliseconds, against roughly 600 milliseconds for Hughes's geostationary system.
- Streaming pay TV sold by a satellite brand, such as DirecTV's internet service, is a virtual MVPD, covered in PPC Land's vMVPD explainer.
- Digital terrestrial television (DTT), such as Freeview in Britain, comes from ground transmitters through a rooftop aerial rather than a dish.
Recent developments
DirecTV stopped offering satellite to new customers in some markets in June 2025, steering them to streaming, according to Cord Cutters News. Sky, by contrast, extended its contract for SES capacity at 28.2 degrees East into the 2030s on September 30, 2026. "Satellite continues to play an important role in how we deliver our services to customers across the UK and Ireland," said Nick Herm, Sky's group chief operating officer, according to ISPreview. Sky is moving with NBCUniversal in the spin-off Comcast announced on June 29, 2026.
Dish DBS, the company behind Dish TV and Sling TV, filed a prepackaged Chapter 11 case on June 30, 2026 after a delayed spectrum sale to AT&T left it short of cash. It emerged on October 1, 2026, cutting about $4.35 billion of debt, according to Light Reading. Hughes Satellite Systems filed separately on August 2, 2026.
DirecTV Advertising became the first MVPD to join LiveRamp's Conversions API Hub on April 16, 2026, and Magnite named it as a source of addressable TV supply for AI buying agents on September 16, 2026.

- July 10, 1962: Telstar 1 launches and relays the first live transatlantic television that month
- September 30, 1975: HBO delivers the "Thrilla in Manila" to cable systems by satellite
- 1985: Programmers begin scrambling satellite feeds received by C-band dishes
- 1988: The Satellite Home Viewer Act creates the distant-signal copyright licence
- December 11, 1988: SES launches Astra 1A
- February 5, 1989: Sky Television launches its four-channel satellite package
- November 2, 1990: Sky and British Satellite Broadcasting merge to form BSkyB
- December 17, 1993: Hughes launches the first DirecTV satellite
- June 17, 1994: DirecTV signs its first customer
- December 28, 1995: EchoStar I launches; Dish Network service follows in March 1996
- November 1999: The Satellite Home Viewer Improvement Act permits local-into-local service
- October 31, 2002: The Department of Justice sues to block the EchoStar-Hughes merger
- March 2005: DVB-S2 is ratified as ETSI EN 302 307
- 2012: Cablevision, DirecTV and Dish launch commercial household addressable advertising; networks sue Dish over AutoHop in May
- January 2014: Sky launches AdSmart
- March 2014: DVB-S2X is published
- December 20, 2019: The Television Viewer Protection Act makes the distant-signal licence permanent
- September 30, 2024: DirecTV agrees to acquire Dish and Sling TV; the deal is terminated on November 22, 2024
- June 2025: DirecTV stops selling satellite to new customers in some markets
- July 2, 2025: TPG completes its acquisition of AT&T's 70 per cent stake in DirecTV
- June 30, 2026: Dish DBS files a prepackaged Chapter 11 case
- August 2, 2026: Hughes Satellite Systems files for Chapter 11
- September 30, 2026: Sky extends its SES satellite contract into the 2030s
- October 1, 2026: Dish DBS emerges from Chapter 11

Summary
Who. Satellite fleet operators such as SES lease capacity to pay-TV distributors including DirecTV, owned by TPG, Dish, owned by EchoStar, and Sky, owned by Comcast until its planned spin-off. Their ad sales arms, DirecTV Advertising, Dish Media and Sky Media, sell local and addressable time, while the FCC, Congress and national regulators set carriage and spectrum rules.
What. Television transmitted from geostationary satellites to home dishes, decoded by a set-top box under conditional access. Addressable ads work by caching spots on the box's hard drive because the downlink is identical for every home.
When. Satellite carried cable programming from 1975, small-dish DBS arrived in 1994 in the United States and 1989 in Britain, and the US base has been shrinking for a decade, with Dish DBS restructured in court between June 30 and October 1, 2026.
Where. Across continental footprints, with particular weight in rural America, Britain, Poland and India, where pay DTH still counted 48.56 million subscribers in June 2026.
Why. One satellite reaches millions of homes regardless of terrain, which made it the cheapest way to serve dispersed audiences. Broadband now does much of that job, so operators are moving customers to streaming while keeping satellites for homes that streaming cannot yet reach reliably.
